title: Solar System begins: first solids condense
summary: The oldest Solar System solids, calcium–aluminium-rich inclusions found in meteorites such as Mexico's Allende, condense from the hot solar nebula.
description: A fragment of a cold molecular cloud collapsed to form the proto-Sun, surrounded by a rotating disc of gas and dust known as the solar nebula. The first solids to condense in its hottest inner regions were calcium–aluminium-rich inclusions (CAIs), which uranium–lead dating places at about 4,567.3 million years ago; this age is conventionally taken as the start of the Solar System and of this timeline. CAIs survive in primitive meteorites such as Allende, which fell in Chihuahua, Mexico, in 1969 and is among the best-studied sources of them. Traces of short-lived radioactive isotopes such as aluminium-26 in CAIs show that the nebula had been enriched with freshly made material from massive stars, possibly a nearby supernova.
wikipedia: Formation and evolution of the Solar System

title: Grand Tack: Jupiter wanders inward and back
summary: Jupiter forms early and, in one influential model, drifts in to Mars's orbit before Saturn pulls it back out, starving Mars and stirring the asteroid belt.
description: Isotopic differences between meteorite groups indicate that Jupiter's core grew to some 20 Earth masses within about a million years of the first solids, splitting the disc into inner and outer reservoirs. In the Grand Tack hypothesis, proposed by Kevin Walsh, Alessandro Morbidelli and colleagues in 2011, the young Jupiter then migrated inward through the gas disc to about 1.5 astronomical units, roughly Mars's present distance from the Sun, until Saturn caught up and the two planets, locked in an orbital resonance, reversed course and moved outward, like a sailing boat tacking. Jupiter's excursion would have cleared away much of the rocky material beyond about 1 astronomical unit, explaining why Mars is so small, and mixed rocky and icy bodies into the asteroid belt, where both types are found today. Because the planets could only migrate through gas, this must have happened within the first few million years, before the solar nebula dispersed.
mainstreamView: The Grand Tack is an influential but unconfirmed model. It neatly explains Mars's small mass and the mix of asteroid types, but alternatives reproduce these features without large-scale migration, for example an inner disc that was poor in solids beyond Earth's orbit from the start, or an early instability among the giant planets. Whether Jupiter and Saturn could reverse their migration as required depends on uncertain properties of the gas disc, so planetary scientists regard the question as open.

title: Planetesimals melt and form iron cores
summary: Within a few million years, early planetesimals melt and separate iron cores; iron meteorites such as Namibia's Hoba are fragments of them.
description: Dust in the solar nebula clumped into planetesimals kilometres to hundreds of kilometres across within roughly the first million years. Heat from the decay of aluminium-26 melted the earliest-formed bodies, letting molten metal sink into cores, which hafnium–tungsten dating shows happened within about one to three million years of the first solids. When later collisions shattered these bodies, their cores became iron meteorites; the roughly 60-tonne Hoba meteorite in Namibia, the largest known, is one such fragment. Isotopic differences between meteorite groups also suggest that Jupiter's core grew during this period, separating inner and outer reservoirs of the disc. Collisions among planetesimals built the larger planetary embryos from which Earth later assembled.

title: Solar nebula gas disperses
summary: Within about four million years of the first solids, the solar nebula's gas is gone, closing the window for giant planets to capture gas.
description: The gas of the protoplanetary disc did not last long: it was accreted onto the young Sun or driven off by its radiation and winds. Palaeomagnetic measurements of angrite meteorites, including D'Orbigny, found on a farm in Buenos Aires Province, Argentina, in 1979, indicate that the nebula's magnetic field, and hence its gas, had vanished by about 3.8 million years after the first solids formed. Jupiter and Saturn must therefore have gathered their massive gas envelopes before then. Earth, by contrast, continued to grow for tens of millions of years through collisions among rocky bodies in a largely gas-free disc.

title: Exploded planet: Phaeton and Sitchin's Tiamat
dateLabel: Claimed; shown as the asteroid belt forms
summary: An old idea that the asteroid belt is the wreckage of a lost planet, Phaeton, resurfaced in Zecharia Sitchin's claim that Earth is half of a shattered Tiamat.
description: After discovering the asteroid Pallas in 1802, the German astronomer Heinrich Olbers of Bremen suggested that it and Ceres were fragments of a planet that had once orbited between Mars and Jupiter, where the Titius–Bode law predicted one, and had been destroyed by a collision or explosion; the lost world was later dubbed Phaeton, after the son of the sun god Helios in Greek myth. The idea was respectable in the 19th century and encouraged the search for more asteroids, but fell from favour as the small total mass of the belt became clear. In the late 20th century the American astronomer Tom Van Flandern revived it as an 'exploded planet hypothesis', arguing that asteroids and comets came from planets that had blown apart. Zecharia Sitchin's 1976 book The 12th Planet gave it a mythological form, claiming that ancient Mesopotamian texts describe a collision between moons of a wandering planet, Nibiru, and a planet called Tiamat, whose broken halves became Earth and the asteroid belt.
mainstreamView: The whole asteroid belt contains only about 3% of the mass of the Moon, far too little to be the remains of a planet, and meteorites from it come from many different parent bodies with distinct compositions and formation ages spread over millions of years, not from one shattered world. Simulations show that Jupiter's gravity stirred up this region, preventing a planet from forming there and removing most of its original material. Earth's own formation by accretion is dated by radiometric methods, and in the Babylonian creation epic Enuma Elish, Tiamat is a primordial sea goddess, not a planet; nothing in Mesopotamian texts describes Nibiru as a planet that collided with her.

title: Earth forms by accretion
summary: Collisions between planetesimals and planetary embryos assemble Earth, which has gathered most of its mass by about 4.54 billion years ago.
description: In the gas-free inner Solar System, rocky planetesimals and planetary embryos ranging from the size of the Moon to that of Mars collided and merged over tens of millions of years to build Earth and the other rocky planets. Earth's age of 4.54 ± 0.05 billion years comes from radiometric dating of meteorites that formed alongside it, an approach established by Clair Patterson's lead-isotope work in 1956, and is consistent with the oldest terrestrial and lunar samples. Because accretion was gradual and the planet's earliest surface has been destroyed, there is no single birth date: the figure marks the stage when Earth had gathered most of its mass. Heat from impacts and radioactive decay kept much of the young planet molten.

title: Young-Earth creationist chronology
summary: Young-Earth creationism holds that Earth was created only about 6,000–10,000 years ago, based on a literal reading of the Book of Genesis.
description: Calculations of the world's age from biblical genealogies have a long history in Jewish and Christian scholarship; the best known, by James Ussher, Archbishop of Armagh, placed the Creation in 4004 BC in a work published in 1650. Modern young-Earth creationism, revived in the 20th century by works such as John Whitcomb and Henry Morris's The Genesis Flood (1961), holds that the universe, Earth and life were created in six days a few thousand years ago and that much of the rock record was laid down by Noah's Flood. It is a sincerely held belief for many people, particularly in some evangelical Protestant communities, while many other religious traditions and denominations accept an ancient Earth. It appears here, at the scientific date of Earth's formation, because it is a claim about that event.
mainstreamView: Independent radiometric methods, including uranium–lead, lead–lead, samarium–neodymium and rubidium–strontium dating, consistently date meteorites to about 4.567 billion years, the oldest terrestrial minerals to 4.4 billion years and Earth itself to 4.54 ± 0.05 billion years. Annual layers in ice cores and lake sediments alone can be counted back tens of thousands of years, and radioactive decay rates have been shown to stay constant under geological conditions. Features such as stacked ancient soils, fossil reefs, thick evaporite deposits and slowly accumulated deep-sea sediments also require very long timescales. For these reasons geologists and the world's scientific academies conclude that a young Earth is incompatible with the evidence.

title: Abiogenic oil: Thomas Gold's deep-Earth gas
dateLabel: Claimed: hydrocarbons trapped as Earth accreted
summary: Astrophysicist Thomas Gold argued that oil and gas are not fossil fuels but primordial hydrocarbons, trapped as Earth formed and still seeping up from the deep.
description: Ideas that petroleum can form without living matter go back to the 19th century, when the chemist Dmitri Mendeleev proposed that it arose from reactions of metal carbides deep underground, and a school of Soviet geologists developed a theory of deep, abiotic oil in the mid-20th century. From the late 1970s the Austrian-born astrophysicist Thomas Gold of Cornell University championed a Western version, arguing that Earth accreted carbon-rich material like that of carbonaceous meteorites and that hydrocarbons trapped since the planet's formation continually migrate upward. He explained the biological molecules found in oil as contamination by microbes living deep in the crust, which he called the 'deep hot biosphere'. At his urging, a borehole was drilled more than 6 kilometres into the Siljan Ring, an ancient impact structure in central Sweden, in the late 1980s, but it recovered only small amounts of oily material whose origin was disputed.
mainstreamView: Petroleum geologists overwhelmingly conclude that commercial oil and most natural gas formed from the buried remains of plankton, algae and plants, slowly heated over millions of years in sedimentary basins. Oil contains molecular fossils, or biomarkers, such as steranes and hopanes that derive from the cell membranes of particular groups of organisms, and oil fields are found in or beside sedimentary source rocks with a suitable burial history. Small amounts of methane and other simple hydrocarbons do form without life, for example where seawater reacts with mantle rock at vents such as Lost City, but no commercially significant abiotic oil deposit has been found, and critics attributed the Siljan material to drilling fluids or nearby sediments. Gold's separate idea of a deep biosphere, by contrast, has been borne out by the discovery of microbes living kilometres below the surface.

title: Earth's iron core separates
summary: Molten iron and nickel sink through the hot young Earth to form its core, a separation largely complete within a few tens of millions of years.
description: As Earth grew, energy from impacts and radioactive decay melted much of it, allowing dense metallic iron and nickel to sink through the silicate mantle and collect at the centre, a process sometimes called the iron catastrophe. Hafnium–tungsten isotope dating indicates that most of the core segregated within roughly 30 to 100 million years of the first Solar System solids, largely in step with accretion, with the Moon-forming impact adding a final episode. The sinking metal released enormous gravitational energy, heating the planet further, and carried iron-loving elements such as gold and platinum into the core. Exact timings depend on how completely the metal of incoming impactors mixed with Earth's mantle, which is still debated.

title: Hollow Earth: Halley's concentric shells
summary: Edmond Halley proposed in 1692 that Earth is a hollow shell around concentric inner spheres; later writers added polar openings and inhabited inner worlds.
description: To explain why the direction of Earth's magnetic field slowly drifts, the astronomer Edmond Halley suggested in a paper to the Royal Society in London in 1692 that Earth consists of an outer shell about 500 miles thick enclosing two concentric inner shells and a central core, each turning at a slightly different rate and perhaps even inhabited. He was encouraged by Isaac Newton's estimate, later shown to be wrong, that the Moon was denser than Earth, which seemed to allow Earth's interior to be partly empty. In the 19th century John Cleves Symmes Jr. added great openings at the poles, and later novelists, occultists and conspiracy theorists imagined habitable inner worlds lit by a central sun. It appears here, when Earth's dense iron core actually formed, because it is a claim about the planet's internal structure.
mainstreamView: Earth is not hollow. Henry Cavendish's 1798 experiment showed that its mean density is about 5.5 grams per cubic centimetre, roughly twice that of surface rocks, so the interior must be much denser than the crust. Seismic waves from earthquakes reveal a rocky crust and mantle, a liquid iron outer core and a solid inner core, identified by Inge Lehmann in 1936, and Earth's moment of inertia confirms that its mass is concentrated toward the centre. Aircraft and satellites have shown that there are no polar openings.

title: Theia impact forms the Moon
summary: In the leading hypothesis, a Mars-sized protoplanet, Theia, strikes the young Earth a glancing blow; debris flung into orbit gathers into the Moon.
description: According to the giant-impact hypothesis, proposed in the mid-1970s by William Hartmann and Donald Davis and independently by Alastair Cameron and William Ward, a body about the size of Mars, later named Theia, struck the proto-Earth at an oblique angle. Debris thrown into orbit, drawn largely from the impactor and Earth's mantle, coalesced into the Moon, explaining its small iron core, its depletion in volatile elements and the large angular momentum of the Earth–Moon system. Published estimates of the timing range from about 4.52 to 4.4 billion years ago, but lunar zircons about 4.46 billion years old, if correctly dated, require the Moon to have formed by then, favouring the older end of that range. Because Earth and Moon rocks are isotopically almost identical, variants such as a higher-energy impact producing a vaporised 'synestia', or a series of smaller impacts, are actively studied.

title: Fission hypothesis: Moon spun off from Earth
summary: George Darwin proposed in 1879 that a fast-spinning, molten Earth flung off the Moon; others later suggested the Pacific basin was the scar.
description: George Darwin, an astronomer and son of Charles Darwin, used tidal theory to show that the Moon had once been much closer to Earth and argued that it had separated from a rapidly rotating, molten planet whose spin was amplified by resonance with solar tides. In 1882 the geologist Osmond Fisher suggested that the Pacific Ocean basin was the scar left behind. Later versions, notably by John O'Keefe and Alan Binder, kept the idea alive into the Apollo era because the Moon's low density resembled that of Earth's iron-poor mantle. Once a respectable scientific hypothesis, it is shown here as superseded rather than as pseudoscience.
mainstreamView: To shed a Moon-sized body, Earth would have needed a rotation period of only about two to three hours, requiring more angular momentum than the Earth–Moon system possesses. Apollo samples showed the Moon is strongly depleted in volatile elements compared with Earth's mantle, which simple fission does not explain, and the Pacific seafloor is less than about 200 million years old, created by plate tectonics, so it cannot be a 4.5-billion-year-old scar. The giant-impact hypothesis explains these observations and replaced fission from the 1980s, although some high-energy impact models echo it by forming the Moon from material spun off a fast-rotating, post-impact Earth.

title: Capture hypothesis: Moon seized by Earth
summary: A once-popular idea held that the Moon formed elsewhere in the Solar System and was later captured intact by Earth's gravity.
description: The capture hypothesis was advanced by the American astronomer Thomas Jefferson Jackson See in the early 1900s and developed from the 1950s by Horst Gerstenkorn, Harold Urey and Hannes Alfvén, among others. It appealed because it could account for the Moon's low density and for chemical differences then thought to exist between the Moon and Earth. Proposed mechanisms included a close encounter in which tides, or drag from debris or an extended atmosphere around Earth, slowed the passing Moon enough to trap it. Like the fission and 'sister-planet' co-accretion models, it lost favour after Apollo samples were analysed in the 1970s and is now regarded as superseded.
mainstreamView: Capturing a body as massive as the Moon requires removing a great deal of orbital energy during a single close pass, and simulations show that such encounters far more often end in collision or escape than in a stable orbit. Most decisively, Apollo samples revealed that the Moon's oxygen, titanium and tungsten isotope ratios are nearly identical to those of Earth's mantle, whereas bodies formed elsewhere in the Solar System, such as Mars and most meteorite parent bodies, differ measurably. A captured, independently formed Moon would not be expected to share this kinship, so planetary scientists favour the giant-impact model.

title: Global magma ocean
summary: The Moon-forming impact melts much of Earth's mantle, leaving a planet-wide ocean of molten rock beneath a dense steam atmosphere.
description: Energy from accretion, core formation and above all the Moon-forming impact melted much of Earth's mantle, leaving a global ocean of molten silicate rock perhaps hundreds to thousands of kilometres deep. Blanketed by a thick atmosphere of steam and carbon dioxide that trapped heat, it may have taken anywhere from a few million to around 100 million years to solidify. As it crystallised, it set the initial layering and chemistry of the mantle and released the gases that formed Earth's early atmosphere. Earlier large impacts probably produced shorter-lived magma oceans too. No rocks survive from this stage, so its depth and duration are inferred from physical models and isotopic signatures of early mantle differentiation.

title: Moon looms close; days perhaps 5 hours long
summary: The newborn Moon orbits more than ten times closer than today, raising huge tides on an Earth whose day may last only about five hours.
description: The Moon probably accreted just a few Earth radii away, within some 20,000–30,000 kilometres, compared with about 384,400 kilometres today. The young Earth spun much faster than now, with a day that may have lasted only around five hours, although the figure depends on the details of the giant impact. The nearby Moon raised tides in Earth's molten and later watery surface far stronger than any today. Tidal friction steadily transferred angular momentum from Earth's spin to the Moon's orbit, slowing Earth's rotation and pushing the Moon outward, a process that continues at about 3.8 centimetres per year.

title: Outgassing builds an early atmosphere
summary: Gases released from the magma ocean, volcanoes and impacts form a thick steam-and-carbon-dioxide atmosphere with no free oxygen.
description: Any thin envelope of hydrogen and helium that Earth captured from the solar nebula was lost early, and a secondary atmosphere formed instead from gases escaping the cooling magma ocean and volcanoes and from volatile-rich impactors. It was at first dominated by water vapour and carbon dioxide, with nitrogen and smaller amounts of other gases, and its surface pressure was probably many times today's. It contained essentially no free oxygen, which accumulated only about 2.4 billion years ago. As the surface cooled, most of the steam rained out to form oceans, leaving a dense carbon dioxide and nitrogen atmosphere whose exact composition, particularly its content of hydrogen and methane, is still debated.

title: Moon's magma ocean crystallises; highlands form
summary: The Moon's global ocean of molten rock cools; light feldspar crystals float to the top and build the pale anorthosite crust of the lunar highlands.
description: The heat of the Moon's rapid assembly after the giant impact melted its outer few hundred kilometres or more into a lunar magma ocean. As it cooled, dense olivine and pyroxene crystals sank to form the lunar mantle, while lighter plagioclase feldspar floated to the surface and built a crust of anorthosite, the pale rock of the highlands visible from Earth. The last dregs of melt, rich in potassium, rare-earth elements and phosphorus (KREEP), were trapped between crust and mantle. Ferroan anorthosite such as Apollo 16 sample 60025, collected by John Young and Charles Duke in 1972 and curated at NASA's Johnson Space Center in Houston, gives ages of about 4.36 billion years, while lunar zircons point to crystallisation under way by about 4.46 billion years ago. How long solidification took, from tens to more than a hundred million years, is debated, and some researchers think the youngest anorthosite ages record later reheating or magmatism instead.

title: Late veneer of meteoritic material
summary: After its core formed, Earth sweeps up a final veneer of meteoritic material, about 0.5% of its mass, that restocks the mantle's gold and platinum.
description: Core formation should have stripped Earth's mantle of almost all highly siderophile, or iron-loving, elements such as gold, platinum, iridium and osmium, yet they occur in the mantle at higher concentrations than expected and in roughly the same relative proportions as in chondritic meteorites. The leading explanation is that after the core had formed and the Moon-forming impact had occurred, Earth accreted a late veneer of chondrite-like material amounting to roughly half a percent of its mass, which mixed into the mantle. This late accretion may also have added some water, carbon and other volatiles, although isotopic evidence suggests it was not the main source of Earth's oceans. Its timing and extent are not precisely known, and alternative explanations, such as changes in how metal and silicate share these elements at high pressure, have been proposed.

title: Oldest known Earth mineral: Jack Hills zircon
summary: A zircon crystal from Western Australia's Jack Hills, dated to 4.404 billion years, is the oldest known fragment of Earth.
description: In 2001 Simon Wilde and colleagues reported a detrital zircon grain that crystallised 4,404 ± 8 million years ago and was later eroded and redeposited in a conglomerate laid down about 3 billion years ago. Zircon is extremely durable and incorporates uranium but excludes lead when it forms, making it a precise geological clock, and thousands of Hadean grains have since been recovered from the Jack Hills. Their oxygen isotopes and mineral inclusions suggest that some Hadean crust was granite-like and had interacted with liquid water at relatively low temperatures within about 150 million years of Earth's formation. How much continental crust existed then, and whether a form of plate tectonics operated, remain debated.

title: First oceans condense
summary: As the surface cools, water vapour rains out into Earth's first oceans, which zircon evidence suggests existed by about 4.4–4.3 billion years ago.
description: Once the magma ocean had solidified and the steam atmosphere had cooled enough, water vapour condensed into a global ocean, kept liquid at high temperatures by the dense atmosphere above it. Elevated oxygen-isotope ratios in Jack Hills zircons about 4.4–4.3 billion years old indicate that their parent magmas incorporated rock altered by liquid water near the surface, the basis of the 'cool early Earth' hypothesis. Most of Earth's water probably came from water-bearing material similar to carbonaceous chondrites accreted while the planet was forming, as hydrogen isotope ratios suggest, and comets appear to have contributed little. The early ocean may have covered nearly the whole planet with few emergent landmasses, and the largest impacts may at times have partly vaporised it.

title: Faint young Sun paradox
summary: The young Sun shines only about 70–75% as brightly as today, yet Earth keeps liquid water, a puzzle known as the faint young Sun paradox.
description: Models of stellar evolution indicate that the Sun's luminosity has risen steadily as hydrogen fused into helium in its core, so in the Hadean it shone at only about 70–75% of today's brightness. Under today's atmosphere and reflectivity, that would have kept Earth's oceans frozen until roughly two billion years ago, yet zircon chemistry and Archean sedimentary rocks indicate liquid surface water. Carl Sagan and George Mullen drew attention to the problem in 1972. Proposed solutions include a stronger greenhouse effect from carbon dioxide, methane or hydrogen, a darker surface with fewer clouds or less land, and a brighter, more massive early Sun.
mainstreamView: Most researchers think a stronger greenhouse effect, chiefly from carbon dioxide regulated by the carbonate–silicate weathering cycle and possibly supplemented by methane or hydrogen, kept the surface above freezing. Geochemical estimates of ancient carbon dioxide levels from fossil soils and other proxies are contested, so the exact mix of factors remains debated. A brighter, more massive early Sun is a minority alternative that observations of mass loss from young Sun-like stars have not strongly supported.

title: Nuvvuagittuq rocks: disputed 4.28-billion-year age
summary: Rocks on Hudson Bay's eastern shore in Quebec may be 4.28 billion years old, Earth's oldest, but many geologists date them to about 3.8 billion.
description: The Nuvvuagittuq Greenstone Belt, on the eastern shore of Hudson Bay in northern Quebec, contains unusual 'faux-amphibolite' rocks that Jonathan O'Neil and colleagues dated in 2008 to about 4.28 billion years using neodymium-142, a decay product of the short-lived isotope samarium-146. If correct, they would be the only surviving Hadean rocks and older than the Acasta Gneiss. The faux-amphibolite contains almost no zircon, however, and zircons from felsic rocks within and cutting the belt give ages of only about 3.75–3.8 billion years, a firm minimum age that many geochronologists take as the belt's true age. Whether the neodymium signal records when the rocks formed or was inherited from older Hadean source material is the crux of the dispute.
mainstreamView: Many geochronologists interpret the 4.28-billion-year neodymium-142 age as a mixing signal inherited from older Hadean source rocks rather than the time the rocks crystallised, and prefer the roughly 3.8-billion-year zircon ages. On either view the belt preserves chemical evidence of crust that formed in the Hadean, but the claim that it contains intact Hadean rock remains contested.

title: Hadean zircons of India's Singhbhum Craton
summary: Zircon grains 4.2–4.0 billion years old, preserved inside younger granitic rocks of eastern India, show Hadean crust formed beyond Australia and Canada.
description: In 2018 researchers reported zircon crystals about 4.2 to 4.0 billion years old, inherited as xenocrysts within Paleoarchean granitoid rocks of the Singhbhum Craton in Odisha, eastern India. The grains crystallised in Hadean magmas and were later caught up in younger melts, surviving after their original host rocks were destroyed. Their hafnium isotopes point to an early-formed, chemically enriched reservoir in the Hadean Earth. Together with rare Hadean grains found in a few other regions, they suggest that crust formation was widespread on the Hadean Earth, although nearly all of that crust was later recycled into the mantle.

title: Earliest magnetic field? Jack Hills zircon claim
summary: Magnetite specks in Jack Hills zircons have been read as a record of Earth's magnetic field 4.2 billion years ago, but critics doubt the signal is original.
description: Earth's magnetic field is generated by the churning of liquid iron in the outer core, the geodynamo, and it helps shield the atmosphere and surface from the solar wind. In 2015 John Tarduno and colleagues reported that tiny magnetite inclusions in Jack Hills zircons, measured with highly sensitive magnetometers, recorded a magnetic field between about 4.2 and 3.3 billion years ago, implying that a geodynamo was already operating in the Hadean. If correct, the early field would have helped protect Earth's water from being stripped away by the young Sun's intense solar wind. The claim is contested, and the oldest widely accepted record of the field comes from rocks in Greenland's Isua belt about 3.7 billion years old.
mainstreamView: Many palaeomagnetists doubt that the zircons preserve a primary signal. Benjamin Weiss and colleagues showed that the Jack Hills host rocks were reheated and remagnetised long after the zircons formed, and found that much of the magnetite associated with such zircons lies along cracks or formed later. Tarduno's group has defended its results with further measurements, so whether Earth had a magnetic field in the Hadean remains unresolved, although models of the cooling core allow one.

title: Origin of life, possibly in the Hadean
dateLabel: Uncertain; perhaps c. 4.2 billion years ago
summary: Life may arise soon after the first oceans; one 2024 genetic study dates the last universal common ancestor to about 4.2 billion years ago.
description: When and where life began is unknown, but evidence suggests it arose within a few hundred million years of the first oceans. A 2024 study combining genomes with molecular-clock calibrations placed the last universal common ancestor (LUCA) of all living organisms at about 4.2 billion years ago, implying that life, already metabolically sophisticated, was established in the Hadean. Leading hypotheses for the setting include deep-sea alkaline hydrothermal vents, such as the modern Lost City field in the mid-Atlantic shown here as an analogue, and shallow ponds or hot springs on land where wet–dry cycles could concentrate organic molecules. The oldest widely accepted fossil evidence of life, stromatolites in Western Australia, is about 3.5 billion years old, and older claims remain debated.
mainstreamView: Most researchers agree that life existed by about 3.5 billion years ago and probably earlier, but a Hadean origin is not established: no Hadean rocks with unambiguous biosignatures survive, molecular-clock estimates for LUCA carry wide uncertainties, and large impacts may have repeatedly sterilised surface environments. Whether life began at hydrothermal vents, in surface ponds or elsewhere is an open question.

title: Possible life signature in 4.1-billion-year-old zircon
summary: Graphite flecks sealed inside a 4.1-billion-year-old Jack Hills zircon have carbon isotope ratios that could reflect biological activity.
description: In 2015 Elizabeth Bell and colleagues reported graphite inclusions sealed inside a Jack Hills zircon crystal dated to 4.10 billion years. The carbon is enriched in the lighter isotope carbon-12, with a ratio (δ¹³C of about −24‰) typical of carbon fixed by living organisms. Because the graphite is enclosed in an uncracked zircon, it is unlikely to be later contamination. If biological in origin, it would push the record of life back several hundred million years before the oldest widely accepted evidence.
mainstreamView: The result is widely cited but not accepted as proof of life: isotopically light carbon can also form through non-biological processes, for example in hydrothermal systems, or be delivered by meteorites, and a single tiny inclusion cannot reveal the environment in which the carbon originated. Most researchers treat it as intriguing evidence consistent with, but not demonstrating, Hadean life.

title: Late Heavy Bombardment
summary: A proposed surge of asteroid and comet impacts batters the Moon, Earth and the inner planets, though whether it was a true spike is disputed.
description: Radiometric ages of impact-melt rocks returned by the Apollo missions cluster around 3.9 billion years, leading researchers in the 1970s to propose a 'lunar cataclysm', a spike in impacts long after the planets had formed. Earth, a larger target with stronger gravity, would have been struck by many more and larger bodies, repeatedly melting parts of its crust and possibly boiling away parts of the oceans. A favoured trigger was a migration of the giant planets, as in the Nice model, which scattered asteroids and comets inward. Earth's own crater record from this period has been erased, so the evidence comes from the Moon, meteorites and Hadean zircons.
mainstreamView: Whether a distinct spike occurred is now doubtful. Many Apollo samples may be contaminated by ejecta from a single basin, Imbrium, biasing their ages toward 3.9 billion years, while lunar meteorites and re-examined crater records show a broader spread of impact ages. Many researchers now favour a bombardment that declined from the era of planet formation, possibly with a smaller late uptick, although the timing of the giant-planet instability is still argued.
